Fourier and Laplace transforms¶

Back to Operators

The transform operators turn a function of x into a function of a new free variable, the frequency, which you name. The result is a Function: it differentiates, composes and saves, and nothing is computed until you supply a value. When the integrand is an exponential polynomial (sums and products of xⁿ, exp, sin, cos, sinh, cosh, and exp(−a x²) for the whole-line Fourier transform) the result is a closed formula. Otherwise it is an unresolved integral over an infinite range that is evaluated by quadrature when you ask for a number; provenance() tells you which one you got.

Entry point

Meaning

fourier::transform(x, w, convention)

∫ f(x) e^{−iwx} dx over the line

fourier::inverse_transform(w, x, convention)

the inverse, acting on a function of w

fourier::cosine_transform(x, w), sine_transform(x, w)

∫₀^∞ f cos(wx) dx, ∫₀^∞ f sin(wx) dx

laplace::transform(x, s)

∫₀^∞ f(x) e^{−sx} dx

laplace::inverse_transform(s, x, terms)

Talbot inversion: a sum of terms/2 evaluations of F, no quadrature

convolution(x, kernel)

∫ f(t) k(x − t) dt

fourier::Convention is Angular (no prefactor forward, 1/2π inverse), Unitary (1/√2π both ways) or Ordinary (frequency in cycles, phase 2πξx).

operators::Operator operators::fourier::transform(std::string_view variable, std::string_view frequency, Convention convention = Convention::Angular);
operators::Operator operators::fourier::inverse_transform(std::string_view frequency, std::string_view variable, Convention convention = Convention::Angular);
operators::Operator operators::laplace::transform(std::string_view variable, std::string_view frequency);
operators::Operator operators::laplace::inverse_transform(std::string_view frequency, std::string_view variable, std::int64_t terms = 32);
operators::Operator operators::convolution(std::string_view variable, math::Function kernel);

The closed forms hold inside the region of convergence (Re s above every exponent, a positive Gaussian coefficient); outside it they are the analytic continuation.

A table lookup and a lazy integral¶

The transform of e^{−x²/2} is √(2π) e^{−w²/2}, and the Laplace transform of x e^{−x/2} cos 3x is Re 1/(s + ½ − 3i)²; both are exponential polynomials, so both come back as formulas. 1/(1+x) is not, so its Laplace transform stays an integral, evaluated at s = 1 to e·E₁(1) = 0.5963….

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace math = pluss::math;
namespace fourier = pluss::operators::fourier;
namespace laplace = pluss::operators::laplace;
using namespace pluss::tils;

static const char *kind(const math::Function &f) { return f.provenance() == math::Provenance::Quadrature ? "lazy integral" : "closed form"; }

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(8));
  const math::Function gauss = math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function x) { return (-(x * x) * 0.5).exp(); });
  const math::Function damped = math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function x) { return x * (-x * 0.5).exp() * (x * 3.0).cos(); });
  const math::Function rational = math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function x) { return 1.0 / (x + 1.0); });

  const math::Function spectrum = fourier::transform("x", "w")(gauss);
  const math::Function L = laplace::transform("x", "s")(damped);
  const math::Function Lr = laplace::transform("x", "s")(rational);
  const auto w = pluss::make_series(0.7), s = pluss::make_series(2.0), one = pluss::make_series(1.0);

  out.writeln("Fourier of a Gaussian   ", spectrum.real()({w}).item<double>(), "  exact ", std::sqrt(2 * std::acos(-1.0)) * std::exp(-0.245), "  ", kind(spectrum));
  out.writeln("Laplace of x e^-x/2 cos ", L({s}).item<double>(), "  exact ", (1.0 / std::pow(std::complex<double>(2.5, -3.0), 2)).real(), "  ", kind(L));
  out.writeln("Laplace of 1/(1+x)      ", Lr({one}).item<double>(), "  exact 0.59634736  ", kind(Lr));
}

Output

Fourier of a Gaussian    1.96194933   exact  1.96194933    closed form
Laplace of x e^-x/2 cos  -0.01182478   exact  -0.01182478    closed form
Laplace of 1/(1+x)       0.59634736   exact 0.59634736   lazy integral

Inversion and convolution¶

laplace::inverse_transform returns a formula in t built from F itself, so it is exact to rounding for a function such as 1/(s+1)², whose inverse is t e^{−t}. The convolution of two Gaussians e^{−x²/2} is √π e^{−x²/4}.

#include <pluss/ma.h>
#include <pluss/tils/aux/output.h>

namespace math = pluss::math;
namespace operators = pluss::operators;
using namespace pluss::tils;

int main() {
  OutputEngine out;
  out.print_defaults(PrintOptions{}.fixed(8));
  const math::Function F = math::function({"s"}, [](math::Function s) { return 1.0 / ((s + 1.0) * (s + 1.0)); });
  const operators::Operator invert = operators::laplace::inverse_transform("s", "t");   // staged
  const math::Function f = invert(F);
  for (const double t : {0.5, 2.0}) out.writeln("f(", t, ") = ", f({pluss::make_series(t)}).item<double>(), "   t e^-t = ", t * std::exp(-t));

  const math::Function gauss = math::function({"x"}, [](math::Function x) { return (-(x * x) * 0.5).exp(); });
  const math::Function conv = operators::convolution("x", gauss)(gauss);                 // compact
  out.writeln("(g*g)(1) = ", conv({pluss::make_series(1.0)}).item<double>(), "   sqrt(pi) e^-1/4 = ", std::sqrt(std::acos(-1.0)) * std::exp(-0.25));
}

Output

f( 0.50000000 ) =  0.30326533    t e^-t =  0.30326533
f( 2.00000000 ) =  0.27067057    t e^-t =  0.27067057
(g*g)(1) =  1.38038845    sqrt(pi) e^-1/4 =  1.38038845

Limits to know¶

  • A transform of a transform that is itself an integral nests two quadratures and may not converge; build the inverse from a formula.

  • Talbot inversion needs t > 0, and poles on the imaginary axis lose accuracy as t grows (raise terms).

  • Transform operators evaluate on the CPU.

  • They save and load (Saving and loading) except convolution, which holds a kernel.
